@C_Barraud's Morning Brief today packed as always and included a Bloomberg story noting the S&P 500 is set to match its choppiest streak since the 2022 bear market with four straight weeks with a move of at least 2.5% in either direction: −2.7%, +2.5%, −8.6% (the worst week since April 2025) and +3.9% so far this week.

Streaks like this look like a bear market thing, so I ran it back to 1928 to see how often they happen outside one.

▪️ There have been 39 prior streaks of four or more straight 2.5%+ weeks. 33 came during bear markets, defined as a 20%+ decline, counted from the prior peak until a new high (the way Bloomberg shades them).
▪️ The six exceptions were August 1929, October 1955, October 1989, September 1997, October 1999 and February 2000. If this week holds, it would be the first four-week streak outside a bear market in nearly 27 years. The S&P would need to fall more than 1.4% in Friday's half session for it not to hold.
▪️ Five weeks is where the line really gets drawn. All 21 streaks that reached five weeks came during bear markets, including all six since 1950 (1962, 1973, 1974, 2008, 2009 and 2022).
▪️ The bear wasn't always obvious at the time, though. When the 1973 streak hit four weeks, the S&P was only 14% off its high. The streak ran to seven weeks, and the decline ended up at 48%.

What came next is mixed. After the six streaks outside a bear, the S&P was higher a month later every time, with a median gain of +3.9%. A year later, though, the median was −1.0%, and only three of six were higher. For all weeks since 1928, the median one-year gain is +9.6%, with 70% higher. Two of those streaks, August 1929 and February 2000, came within about five weeks of major tops. October 1989 came before the 1990 decline that stopped just short of a bear market (−19.9%).

Streaks during bear markets tended to show up nearer the lows. Their median one-year gain was +14.9%, or +17.8% since 1950, with eight of nine higher.

The sample is small, but if history is a guide, next week matters. A fifth straight 2.5%+ week would either be the first outside a bear market in nearly a century of data, or a sign this is more than a correction.

The day after Thanksgiving is usually one of the quietest sessions of the year for stocks, but before you decide to overindulge, note that’s not normally the case when the VIX is elevated heading in.

Since 1990, the S&P 500’s post-Thanksgiving session has normally been tame, with an average intraday range of 0.7%, vs. 1.2% for all days.

But when the VIX is above 20 heading in (14 years), that average range expands to 1.0%, and 8 of the 10 most volatile post-Thanksgiving sessions have come with the VIX over 20.

With the VIX at 25 or higher (6 years), it’s even more so: a 1.3% average range, with 5 of the 6 ranking among the 10 most volatile sessions.

Direction has been a literal coin flip: higher in 7 of the 14 high-VIX years.

Context: Wednesday’s VIX close of 28.3 was the 4th-highest heading into Thanksgiving since 1990 (behind 2008, 2011 and 1997).

Goldman Sachs says "investor uncertainty regarding the earnings outlook creates a wide distribution of potential near-term outcomes for the equity market," and lays out how wide that range is.

▪️ Downside: Apply the 30-year average P/E of 17x to trend EPS of $340 and you get roughly 5,800 on the S&P 500. That would be about 13x–14x consensus 2027 earnings, "similar to the trough forward P/E in 2018 and 2020."
▪️ Upside: If investors "gain confidence in the consensus earnings forecast" and the multiple recovers to its 10-year average of 19x, the index would rise to a new high of 8,100.

Measured against Wednesday's 7,183 close:

▪️ 5,800 is 19.3% below here and 25.8% below the October 6 record of 7,819, well into bear market territory. The index hasn't closed that low since May 2025.
▪️ 8,100 is 12.8% above here and 3.6% above the prior record.
▪️ Goldman's trend EPS of $340 is about 8% below 2026 consensus ($370) and 20% below 2027 consensus ($425), so the downside case is really a call that the consensus numbers are too high.

What stands out in Goldman's P/E chart is that the forward multiple had already fallen from 23x in late 2025 to about 16x, yet the S&P is roughly 5% higher than it was then. So the market has for a while now declined to pay for the consensus numbers.  

Also note the skew: the downside move (−19%) is bigger than the upside move (+13%), though Goldman doesn't put odds on either.The derating has come from earnings estimates rising much faster than prices, not from stocks selling off.

@C_Barraud's Wednesday Brief paired two Japan stories that pull the Bank of Japan in opposite directions:

▪️ Inflation: Japan's services producer price index rose 4.2% year-over-year in October, the fastest since 1990 (Reuters), well above the 3.6% expected.
▪️ Economic Strain: in a Teikoku Databank survey of more than 10,000 firms, 58.5% now say higher rates hurt them more than they help (Bloomberg). That's up 14.2 points from December and from 37.7% in April 2024. Just 2.6% say the net effect is positive.

In the Teikoku survey 47.7% of firms say their main bank has raised their loan rate or proposed raising it. Real estate is hit hardest (71.4%). Retail saw the biggest jump (up 20.8 points to 64.8%), as higher rates squeeze both its own borrowing costs and its customers. 16.3% plan to cut or delay capex.

Former board member Seiji Adachi told Reuters he expects a hike to 1.5% in December or January, and possibly to 1.75% or 2% next year. But he warned that consumption is "moving below recent years' trend," which could push PM Takaichi's government to resist further hikes. The economy already shrank in Q3 as consumption slumped, and two board members dissented on September's hike.

One more wrinkle: the most common response to higher rates, at 33% of firms, is passing the cost on in prices. So the hikes may be feeding some of the very inflation the BOJ is fighting. That makes the path beyond 1.5% look less certain than analysts' 1.75% to 2% terminal-rate calls suggest.

Treasury closes a mixed week with a mixed auction:

Wednesday’s $44 billion 7-year auction saw dealers take the least since July 2025, but it still tailed (yield above expectations) by 1.0 basis point, the most since May 2024.

Indirect bidders (which include foreign buyers) stayed below their six-month average, and direct bidders took the second-largest share on record. That comes after a solid 2-year Monday but a 5-year Tuesday that tailed for a 13th straight time.

▪️ Indirect: 58.2% vs. 57.8% in October and a 63.6% six-month average. That’s the 11th straight note or bond auction with the indirect share below its six-month average.

▪️ Direct: 33.2%, second-highest since bidder data began in 2008 (record: 33.7%, July 2025), vs. 32.8% in October and a 24.6% six-month average.

▪️ Dealers: 8.6%, lowest since July 2025, vs. 9.4% in October and an 11.7% six-month average.

▪️ Bid-to-cover: 2.43, lowest since September, vs. 2.46 in October and a 2.48 six-month average.

▪️ Tail: +1.0 basis point (4.708% high yield vs. 4.698% when-issued), biggest since May 2024, vs. on the screws in October and a +0.1 six-month average.

▪️ High yield: 4.708%, lowest since August, vs. 4.894% in October and a 4.586% six-month average.

@investingLive_’s Greg Michalowski graded it a C+, calling it “mixed but still better than average,” with strong direct demand leaving dealers with just 8.6%. ZeroHedge called it “another subpar, tailing auction,” though “not nearly as ugly as yesterday’s 5Y sale.”

I'm less concerned about the weak indirect demand as that may say more about how buyers are categorized than about foreign demand, but demand was mixed. Overall demand was the least since September, but dealers were stuck with the least since last July. The tail seems out of place, but it is what it is. "Mixed" definitely seems to sum it up.

Fed Beige Book (December FOMC), data through November 16

A mixed bag from the November Beige Book, which shows growth narrowing for a third straight report and the price reacceleration stalling. But the growth outlook was raised, wage growth picked up and firms expect "expenses and prices to continue rising," which gives the doves little to push back on ahead of the December meeting.

▪️ Activity: 8 of 12 Districts growing, down from 9 in October and 11 in July, with 4 reporting no change. For a 4th straight report, none declined.
▪️ Prices: rose "moderately overall, as in the prior reporting period." In October, 3 Districts were robust and 4 had a faster pace. No counts this time, but the District highlights have Cleveland and St. Louis still robust and only New York easing.
▪️ Pipeline: a Cleveland manufacturer sees contract prices up 19% at the start of the year, and Richmond manufacturers' annual price growth topped 5% for the first time since 2023.
▪️ Wages: "rose moderately, an uptick from modest increases" in October, driven partly by cost-of-living adjustments. Hiring was upgraded slightly to "rose slightly on balance" from "little or no change."
▪️ Consumer: "little changed," with households "increasingly selective." Kansas City firms expect lower spending per customer this holiday season.
▪️ Housing and construction weakened on higher borrowing costs. In Dallas, sales slowed with mortgage rates above 7%.
▪️ Rates: Cleveland clients are locking in rates "ahead of anticipated rate increases," and Dallas bankers warned that "future rate hikes" could hurt loan repayment.
▪️ Outlook: nudged up, though, to "slight to moderate growth" from "slight growth" in October.

US New Home Sales jumped to a 701K annual rate in October, the most since Dec 2025 and above every estimate in Bloomberg's survey. 

The caveats: It's a one-region story fueled by buyers snapping up the least expensive homes and comes only after a big downward revision to September (this report is very volatile with heavy revisions).

▪️ +14.2% m/m, even with mortgage rates peaking at 7.5% in early Oct, the highest in almost three years (Bloomberg). But Sep was cut to 614K from 676K (now −9.7% m/m), so Oct is only 21K above Aug's 680K. The gain is also inside the Census ±22.6% margin of error. As ZeroHedge put it, "it's anyone's guess where this October rebound ends up."
▪️ South +137K to 515K, the biggest one-month gain on record (data to 1973) and the most since Mar 2021. A record 73.5% of all sales.
▪️ The other three regions combined −21.2% to the lowest since Jul 2022. West joint-lowest since Mar 2014, Northeast lowest since Apr 2015.
▪️ Average price $459.9K, lowest since Jul 2021, −12.1% y/y (steepest drop since Apr 2009). Median $391.3K, −3.2% y/y. Bill McBride puts both 15% below their 2022 peaks.
▪️ Under-$300K homes were 25% of sales, the highest share since 2021 (Bloomberg). Builders are leaning "heavily on costly sales incentives."
▪️ Homes for sale 470K, fewest since Aug 2024. Months' supply 8.0, the least since Dec 2025 but above the 4–6 normal for 56 straight months. Since 2000, the median price was lower a year later 72% of the time at this level.
▪️ Under construction 245K, down 5 straight months to the joint-fewest since Jul 2021. McBride says builders are "probably waiting to start some homes until they clear more inventory."

Q3 GDP revision shows the economy was even stronger coming into the fourth quarter than previously thought.

Q3 GDP revised up well more than expected to 4.3% (est 3.5%; advance 3.4%), the fastest pace since Q3 2023. The 0.9-point upgrade was the biggest advance-to-second-estimate revision since Q2 2020, and since Q2 2015 excluding the pandemic.

▪️ Investment drove about half of the upgrade, led by software. Software spending grew 22.3% instead of 9.6% after BEA revised software prices to a 7.0% annualized decline from a 1.6% rise.
▪️ Information processing equipment added 0.95 point to growth, a record in data back to 1947.
▪️ Consumer spending was revised up to 4.2% (est 3.9%; advance 3.8%), the fastest since Q4 2024. Goods were revised up (pharmaceuticals, software, gasoline) and services down, with health care growth cut to 1.3% from 4.9%.
▪️ Final sales to private domestic purchasers were revised up to 5.8%, the most since Q2 2021.
▪️ Trade was still a big drag, with net exports subtracting 3.2 points, the most since Q1 2025.
▪️ The GDP price index was revised down to 1.9% (est 2.3%). PCE prices (2.1%) and core PCE (2.5%, in line) were unrevised.
▪️ Real GDI rose 4.4%, slightly faster than GDP, and the average of the two was also 4.4%, the most since Q4 2023.
▪️ Corporate profits rose $206B to a record $4.92T, up 21.3% from a year ago and a record 14.9% of GDP in data back to 1947. Nonfinancial profit margins were the highest since 1955.
▪️ The saving rate was revised down to 3.9%, the lowest since Q3 2022.

October core PCE prices comes in a touch hot at 3.26% year-over-year, rounding up to a tenth above estimates and the highest since November 2023. Inflation breadth also widened. 

Incomes beat expectations, helped by a one-time Medicare rebate, but real spending slipped and the saving rate rose to 4.1%.

Prices:
▪️ Core +0.29% m/m (est 0.3%); 3.26% y/y (est 3.2%), the highest since November 2023.
▪️ Headline +0.32% (est 0.3%); 3.845% y/y (est 3.8%), the highest since May 2023.
▪️ Core three-month annualized 3.63%, the highest since March.
▪️ Services ex energy & housing 3.64% y/y, the highest since December 2024; three-month annualized 4.27%, the highest since March 2024.
▪️ Energy price index at another record high; gasoline +38.02% y/y.
▪️ Share of 244 components up more than 3% y/y rose to 51.2% from 48.4%, vs the 32% pre-pandemic average Warsh cited.

Incomes:
▪️ Personal income +0.73% (est 0.4%), the most since April 2025, helped by a one-time Medicare premium rebate.
▪️ Real disposable income +0.51%, the most since January.

Spending:
▪️ Nominal +0.28% (est 0.4%); real −0.03% (est 0.1%), the weakest since January.
▪️ Real goods −0.23% (motor vehicles −1.48%); real services +0.05%.
▪️ Saving rate up to 4.1% from a downwardly revised 3.6%, now the lowest since October 2022.

ZeroHedge: "acyclical inflation is now hotter than cyclical… inflation is becoming embedded."

So inflation is re-accelerating while real spending stalls, and households saved a Medicare rebate rather than spending it.
